removed.title: Cross-patient challenge prompts
removed.text:
Use these two prompts during the gallery interrogation phase. Do not resolve them for students — steer toward reasoning tied to the chapter's ideas.

Challenge 1: 'Two patients both need a mineral — the child in the jowar district and the elder in the Himalayan town. Their minerals are different and their sources are very different. Why does the solution look so different for each?' (Target insight: 'local and minimally processed' is not a universal rule; some protective nutrients require fortified or non-plant sources because local soil lacks them. A good comparison is iron from green leafy vegetables, regionally available, versus iodine from iodised salt, processed but necessary.)

Challenge 2: 'One group flagged a food-miles risk in their recommendation. Another group's recommended food travels even further but they did not flag it — should they have?' (Target insight: food-miles reasoning must be applied consistently and weighed against nutritional necessity; students must articulate the trade-off rather than apply a blanket rule.)

If groups are more than five, two groups may share a card and compare recommendations at the gallery stage. During group work, redirect students who chose regionally implausible foods by asking 'What grows there?' and redirect students uncertain about test results by asking 'Which test result tells you fat is present?'

removed.title: Canteen food-sample data strips
removed.text:
Both strips are identical — every group receives the same two items. Results are described by behaviour only; the food is not named.

Item X: When a small piece is pressed on brown paper and held to light, a translucent patch remains. When iodine solution is added to a sample, no blue-black colour appears. When copper sulfate solution and caustic soda are added, a violet-purple colour develops.

Item Y: No translucent patch on paper. When iodine solution is added, the sample turns blue-black. When copper sulfate solution and caustic soda are added, no violet-purple colour appears.

Groups use these results to determine which nutrients (fat, starch, protein) each item contains and decide whether each item belongs on their patient's tray or should be limited.

removed.title: Patient profile cards
removed.text:
Each card is hand-written on an index card or half-sheet. It states the patient's name, age, location and dominant local crop, current typical daily diet, physical activity level, and one observable symptom or health need described in plain language. The card does NOT name the deficiency — students must infer it.

Card 1 — Child, recovering patient, jowar-growing district. Diet is predominantly jowar-based with very little green leafy vegetables or pulses. Low activity (bed rest). Symptom: pale gums and fatigue, tires easily on minor exertion.

Card 2 — Teenager, athlete, coastal fishing village. High physical activity. Diet is rice and fish-based but meals are often skipped before training. Symptom: frequent muscle cramps and slower recovery after exercise.

Card 3 — Elderly person, Himalayan town. Low activity. Diet relies on locally grown cereals and dairy; rarely eats processed or iodised products. Symptom: visible swelling at the front of the neck, sluggishness.

Card 4 — Young mother, sugarcane-farming belt. Moderate activity. Diet is heavy in packaged biscuits, instant noodles, and sweetened drinks; fresh produce is limited. Symptom: persistent tiredness, dry skin, frequent minor infections.

Card 5 — Construction worker, urban area. High physical activity. Skips breakfast and lunch regularly; eats one large meal at night, often fried street food. Symptom: low stamina during work hours, slow wound healing.

periods.activity_description: Students recall and record the foods they have eaten over the past week, then compare their lists with classmates, noticing similarities and differences. The class pools observations to map out the variety of foods eaten across different homes and regions.

roles.role_description: Each student writes a personal food record from memory, then shares selected items aloud for a class tally.
Facilitates the sharing, records items on the board, and draws out patterns and differences across the class.

time_bands.activity: Students independently recall and write down foods eaten over a week, prompted by meal categories (breakfast, lunch, dinner, snacks).
Volunteers share their lists; teacher groups responses on the board under broad headings such as grains, vegetables, dairy, and non-vegetarian items.
Students compare their own list with two neighbours and note one food item unique to each person's record.
Teacher draws attention to the variety observed and poses the question: why do people across India eat such different foods?

periods.teacher_notes: This opening unit sets the stage for the whole chapter by grounding students in their own lived experience of food before any formal content is introduced. Watch for students who treat this as a trivial exercise — encourage them to include traditional or home-cooked items they may consider unremarkable. A good checkpoint is whether students can articulate at least one meaningful difference between their own food list and a classmate's.
materials: Notebooks or loose sheets for food record

periods.activity_description: Groups research the traditional foods and locally grown crops of assigned Indian states — Punjab, Karnataka, and Manipur — and fill a comparison table linking staple dishes to the crops grown in each region. Groups share findings and the class builds a picture of how local agriculture shapes food.

roles.role_description: Each group investigates one assigned state, completing a table of traditional dishes, crops grown, and climate hints from the chapter.
Circulates to prompt groups to connect dishes to crops and to probe the climate–crop–food chain of reasoning.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recaps the variety observed in the previous unit and introduces the task: each group will investigate one state's food.
Groups use the chapter section on food in different regions to complete a three-column table: state, traditional dishes, and main crops grown.
Each group shares their table; teacher compiles a class summary table on the board, highlighting the crop–food link for each state.
Class discusses: what happens to food traditions when a crop fails or a new crop is introduced?

periods.teacher_notes: This unit builds directly on the variety noticed in the previous unit, now giving students a structural explanation — local crops and climate shape food traditions. A common confusion is that students may think food differences are only about taste preference; redirect them to the crop-climate-food chain as the primary driver. Probing question: could Punjab grow ragi as easily as Karnataka? Why or why not?
materials: India map (optional, if available in classroom)

periods.activity_title: From Chulha to Gas Stove: How Cooking Changed
periods.activity_description: Students examine contrasting images of traditional and modern cooking tools — chulha versus gas stove, sil-batta versus electric grinder — and identify what changed and why. The class connects these shifts to technological development, transportation, and communication, and considers what was gained and lost.

roles.role_description: Presents the contrasting image pairs, narrates the historical change, and guides the class through cause-and-effect reasoning.
Each student notes two changes and the reason behind each, then shares one observation with the class.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the image pairs from the chapter and asks students to describe what they see without explanation.
Teacher explains the shift from traditional to modern tools, attributing it to technological development, improved transport, and better communication.
Students individually write two changes they identified and a reason for each, then briefly share with a neighbour.
Class discusses: are any traditional practices being revived today, and why might that happen?

periods.teacher_notes: This unit completes the food diversity stage by adding a temporal dimension — food practices change over time, not just across regions. Students sometimes assume modern is always better; use the discussion question to surface the value of traditional practices, particularly around nutrition and sustainability, which the chapter returns to later. Watch for the misconception that cooking changes happened suddenly — stress that these were gradual shifts driven by multiple factors.
materials: Textbook images of chulha, sil-batta, gas stove, electric grinder
homework: Interview one elderly family member or neighbour about one cooking practice from their childhood that has changed, and note the reason they give for the change.

periods.stage_label: Classify nutrients by function and source
periods.activity_title: The Food Festival Table: Sorting Nutrients
periods.activity_description: Using the Traditional Food Festival setting from the chapter, students receive a list of foods and sort them into nutrient categories — carbohydrates, fats, and proteins — recording both the food item and its function (energy-giving or body-building). Students discover that the same food can supply more than one nutrient.

roles.role_description: Groups sort a provided food list into a nutrient classification table, citing chapter-given functions for each category.
Introduces the nutrient framework and circulates to address early misconceptions about fat being entirely harmful.

time_bands.activity: Teacher sets the scene with the school Traditional Food Festival and asks: why do we feel tired when we skip a meal? Students briefly share ideas.
Groups fill a classification table: food item, nutrient it provides, and function — using chapter content on carbohydrates, fats, and proteins.
Groups share their tables; class notes any food placed in more than one column (e.g., peanuts under both fat and protein).
Teacher summarises carbohydrates and fats as energy-giving foods and proteins as body-building foods, previewing the next unit on vitamins and minerals.

periods.teacher_notes: The jump from the food diversity stage to nutrient classification is natural here — students already know what foods they eat, and now they begin to ask what those foods do. A very common error at this stage is placing all fats in a harmful category; use the laddoo and winter warmth example from the chapter to normalise fat as a necessary energy store. A useful checkpoint: can each group explain in one sentence why growing children need adequate protein?
materials: Prepared food list cards or written list on board (using chapter examples)
Blank three-column classification tables in notebooks

periods.stage_label: Classify nutrients by function and source
periods.activity_title: Vitamins and Minerals: The Protective Pair
periods.activity_description: Students examine the historical cases of scurvy and goitre from the chapter and, working from the nutrient chart, build a two-part classification table — vitamins and minerals — recording sources, functions, and deficiency diseases for each. They identify vitamins and minerals as protective nutrients needed only in small amounts.

roles.role_description: Each student reads the two historical cases and the nutrient chart, then completes their own classification table independently.
Poses questions to connect the historical narrative to the table entries and highlights what 'protective nutrient' means in practice.

time_bands.activity: Students read the scurvy and goitre cases from the chapter and identify: what was missing, what symptom appeared, what fixed it.
Students independently complete a table for all seven vitamins and minerals from Fig. 3.5: nutrient, sources, deficiency disease.
Students compare their tables with a neighbour and resolve any differences using the chapter chart.
Teacher defines protective nutrients and notes that vitamins C and D behave differently — one is destroyed by heat, the other is made by the body.

periods.teacher_notes: The historical cases make the abstract concept of micronutrient deficiency concrete; press students to state the causal chain (missing nutrient → specific disease) rather than just memorising names. A frequent confusion is between rickets (Vitamin D) and beriberi (Vitamin B1) — the chapter distinguishes them clearly through their symptoms, so guide students back to the symptom description. The observation that Vitamin D comes from sunlight, not food alone, often surprises students and is worth dwelling on briefly.

periods.stage_label: Classify nutrients by function and source
periods.activity_description: Students apply the nutrient classification they have built to a real-world survey task: using the chapter's Activity 3.4 design, they examine hypothetical case descriptions of dietary habits and match observed symptoms (from the chapter's deficiency disease list) to likely missing nutrients, then suggest dietary improvements using Indian food sources.

roles.role_description: Groups analyse assigned case descriptions, identify the deficiency, name the missing nutrient, and propose a diet change using chapter-listed foods.
Distributes case descriptions adapted from the chapter's survey activity and facilitates inter-group comparison of recommendations.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the task: each group receives a case describing a person's diet and symptoms, and must identify the deficiency and suggest an improvement.
Groups work through their case, identifying the symptom, matching it to a nutrient deficiency from the chart, and listing two Indian food sources that address it.
Groups present their diagnosis and dietary recommendation; class checks against the chapter chart and discusses whether the food sources are realistic for that region.
Teacher consolidates: nutrients are classified by function and identified by deficiency, and Indian foods provide all essential nutrients if the diet is varied.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit asks students to apply the classification from the previous two units to diagnosis-style reasoning — a meaningful cognitive step up. Watch for groups that jump to a single food fix without checking whether the identified food actually appears in the chapter's source list for that nutrient; anchor all recommendations in the chapter. Connecting the food sources to the regional diversity discussed in stage one (e.g., recommending amla as a Vitamin C source in northern India) makes the arc feel coherent to students.
materials: Prepared case description cards (teacher-authored from chapter content)
homework: Using the nutrient chart, plan one day's meals for a ten-year-old that provides at least one source each of carbohydrate, protein, Vitamin C, and iron — name the specific food for each.

periods.activity_title: The Iodine Test: Hunting for Starch
periods.activity_description: Students perform the iodine test on a set of food samples — potato, boiled rice, cucumber, and oil — and record colour changes, classifying each sample as starch-present or starch-absent. They connect the blue-black colour change to the presence of starch and note which foods confirmed their earlier nutrient classification.

roles.role_description: Groups apply diluted iodine solution to each food sample, observe and record colour changes, and classify results in a table.
Demonstrates the iodine test procedure on one sample before groups begin, and circulates to ensure safe handling of iodine solution.

time_bands.activity: Teacher demonstrates the iodine test on a potato slice, naming the reagent, the procedure, and the positive result to watch for.
Groups test potato, boiled rice, cucumber, and oil, recording colour change and starch presence/absence in their results table.
Groups compare results across the class and note which samples showed a positive test; class reconciles any conflicting results.
Students connect results to the nutrient classification: starch-positive foods were listed as carbohydrate sources in the previous unit.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the testing stage; students transition from classifying nutrients by reading to testing for them by doing. A common error is applying too much iodine, which darkens all samples; instruct groups to use only a small drop. The key insight to check for is that the test identifies the presence of a specific nutrient — starch — not whether a food is 'good' or 'bad', which surfaces a misconception about food testing as judgment.
materials: Diluted iodine solution in dropper bottles
White ceramic tiles or small plates

periods.activity_description: Students perform the paper-patch test on food samples — peanut, butter, boiled rice, and cucumber — pressing each onto plain paper and holding against light to check for a translucent patch, recording and interpreting results. They update their nutrient classification table with empirical test evidence.

roles.role_description: Groups press each food sample onto paper, allow it to dry briefly, hold the paper against light, and record whether a translucent oily patch is visible.
Models the correct amount of pressure to apply and how to judge a translucent patch versus a water stain, which disappears on drying.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models the paper-patch test with one sample, explicitly distinguishing a water stain (fades) from an oily patch (persists).
Groups carry out the test on peanut, butter, boiled rice, and cucumber, recording results in their table alongside the iodine test results from the previous unit.
Groups note that peanut gave a positive fat patch; class discusses whether peanut also tested positive for starch and what this means about a single food containing multiple nutrients.
Students annotate their results table: peanut column now shows fat-present and protein-present (from chapter), illustrating nutrient overlap.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit immediately follows the iodine test, so students are now building a multi-column results table that will culminate after the protein demonstration. The critical teaching moment is the peanut result — it is positive for fat here and will be positive for protein in the next unit, making it the chapter's key example of multi-nutrient foods. Watch for students who interpret a translucent patch on rice as fat; rice is a carbohydrate source and the chapter explicitly states it does not show a positive fat test.

periods.activity_title: The Violet Signal: Testing for Protein
periods.activity_description: The teacher demonstrates the protein test using copper sulfate solution and caustic soda on boiled gram, peanut, and soya bean; students observe the violet colour change and record results. Students complete their three-test comparison table and identify which foods tested positive for multiple nutrients.

roles.role_description: Performs the protein test as a demonstration, narrating each step and the safety reason for keeping the reagents teacher-handled.
Students observe, record the colour outcome for each sample, and complete their comparison table by adding the protein test column.

time_bands.activity: Teacher demonstrates the protein test on boiled gram, narrating the two-step reagent addition (copper sulfate, then caustic soda) and pointing out the violet colour change.
Teacher repeats the demonstration for peanut and soya bean; students record results for all three samples in their tables.
Students complete the full comparison table (Table 3.3 from the chapter) covering all three tests across all samples, then identify foods with multiple positive results.
Class discusses: what does it mean for a food to test positive for both fat and protein, and how does this relate to thinking about food as a source of nutrients?

periods.teacher_notes: This unit completes the three-test sequence; the completed table is the central product of this stage. Emphasise that the demonstration format for this test is deliberate — caustic soda is not safe for students to handle — so accuracy of observation is the skill being practised here, not manipulation of the reagent. A misconception to address: a violet colour in only one test does not make peanut a protein-only food; guide students to read across all columns of their table before drawing conclusions.
materials: Caustic soda solution (teacher-prepared, handle with care)
Test tubes or small glass containers
Students' comparison tables from previous two units
homework: Look at the full comparison table you built across the three testing units. Choose one food that tested positive for two nutrients, and write two sentences explaining what those results tell you about that food's role in a diet.

periods.stage_label: Evaluate dietary quality and food choices
periods.activity_description: Students revisit their week's food record from the first unit, evaluate it against the definition of a balanced diet, identify any nutrients missing or in excess, and produce a written diagnosis explaining what changes would bring the diet into balance.

roles.role_description: Each student annotates their food record, maps each item to the nutrient it provides, identifies gaps, and writes a one-paragraph dietary diagnosis.
Introduces the definition of balanced diet from the chapter and circulates to probe whether students are considering roughage and water alongside the seven nutrients.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the definition of a balanced diet — all essential nutrients, roughage, and water in the right amounts — and notes that individual needs vary by age, activity, and health.
Students annotate their original food record: each food item is tagged to its primary nutrient, and gaps or excesses are circled.
Students write a short dietary diagnosis: which nutrients were well-covered, which were absent or sparse, and what specific food changes would address the gaps.
Two or three volunteers share their diagnosis; class notes that different students have different gaps, reinforcing individual variability in nutritional needs.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit pivots from testing to evaluation, using the food record students made in the very first unit — this callback makes the arc feel intentional and is worth naming explicitly. A common error is treating a balanced diet as simply 'eating all food groups' without attending to quantity or roughage; press students to include water and fibre in their diagnosis. Students who had a very limited or very homogeneous food record may feel self-conscious — frame this as a planning exercise, not a judgment.
materials: Students' week's food records from unit 1

periods.stage_label: Evaluate dietary quality and food choices
periods.activity_description: Students examine the comparative nutritional table for potato wafers versus roasted chana from the chapter, calculate the difference in fat, protein, and fibre values, and evaluate which food better supports a balanced diet. The class connects frequent junk food consumption to obesity and health problems.

roles.role_description: Presents the nutritional comparison table from the chapter, guides the calculation exercise, and explains the concept of empty calories.
Students read the table, calculate differences for each nutrient category, and write one evaluative sentence explaining which food is the better dietary choice and why.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the concept of junk food as high sugar, high fat, low protein, low fibre — and presents the potato wafers versus roasted chana comparison table.
Students calculate the difference in fat (35 g vs 6.26 g), protein (low vs 18.64 g), and dietary fibre (low vs 16.8 g) per 100 g, recording each difference.
Students write one evaluative sentence per nutrient column and one overall conclusion about which food supports a balanced diet.
Class discusses: does this mean potato wafers must never be eaten? Teacher connects moderation and frequency to health outcomes.

periods.teacher_notes: The comparison table makes the abstract concept of junk food concrete and numerically grounded; push students to go beyond 'chana is healthier' to state specifically which nutrient difference matters most and why. A misconception to address is that low calorie always equals healthy — roasted chana has fewer calories but the more important advantage is its protein and fibre content. The moderation discussion at the end prevents the lesson from becoming moralistic while still delivering the nutritional message.
materials: Chapter nutritional comparison table (potato wafers vs roasted chana)

periods.stage_label: Evaluate dietary quality and food choices
periods.activity_description: Students examine the nutrient profile of millets — jowar, bajra, ragi, sanwa — and evaluate them against the balanced diet criteria, identifying why they qualify as nutri-cereals. Groups compare millet cultivation requirements to those of the regional crops explored in stage one, evaluating why millets are suitable across varied climatic zones.

roles.role_description: Groups complete an evaluation table: millet name, nutrients it provides, deficiency diseases it helps prevent, and one climatic zone where it is grown.
Introduces the term nutri-cereal and explains the food fortification sidebar and FSSAI's role in food quality regulation.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces millets using the chapter section and asks: why would a food crop that has been grown in India for centuries suddenly become popular again?
Groups fill an evaluation table for millets: nutrients provided, deficiency diseases addressed, and one regional climate where the millet is cultivated.
Groups share tables; class compares millet nutrient profiles against the earlier food record gaps students identified in the previous unit.
Teacher introduces food fortification and FSSAI as mechanisms society uses to address nutritional gaps at scale.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit connects the nutrient classification work directly to a real Indian food crop, reinforcing that the stage-one food diversity discussion and the stage-two nutrient work are two lenses on the same reality. Students may not recognise ragi or sanwa by name depending on their region — use the chapter's description of widespread cultivation to make the point that millets travel across climatic zones precisely because of their adaptability. Watch for the misconception that millets are inferior or old-fashioned foods; the chapter's framing as nutri-cereals should be reinforced here.
materials: Evaluation table template drawn in notebooks

periods.stage_label: Analyse food systems and health connections
periods.activity_title: From Farm to Plate: Mapping Food Miles
periods.activity_description: Students trace the journey of wheat from farm to chapati using the chapter's step-by-step supply chain, map each stage onto a flow diagram, and calculate the number of steps food travels before reaching them. They then evaluate which steps could be shortened to reduce food miles.

roles.role_description: Groups draw a flow diagram of the wheat-to-chapati supply chain, label each stage, and annotate two steps where food miles could be reduced.
Introduces the concept of food miles, presents the wheat journey from the chapter, and poses the evaluative question about shortening the chain.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces food miles — the total distance food travels from producer to consumer — and asks students to guess how many steps their last meal's main ingredient passed through.
Groups draw a labelled flow diagram of the wheat supply chain from the chapter: farming, threshing and winnowing, storage, grinding and packing, transport, retail, home.
Groups annotate their diagram with two places where the chain could be shortened and one benefit of each shortening (cost, freshness, nutrition, or farmer support).
Groups share their annotated diagrams; teacher connects shorter supply chains to both personal health (fresher food) and environmental health (lower pollution).

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the final analytical stage, broadening from what nutrients food contains to how food choices affect systems beyond the individual. Students often find the food miles concept engaging because it connects their food to geography and economics. A common error is focusing only on transport distance and missing the nutrient-loss argument — the chapter argues that fresher food is more nutritious, which links this unit directly back to the vitamin-loss discussion from stage two. Probing question: which of the supply chain steps could a family or school canteen eliminate by buying locally?

periods.stage_label: Analyse food systems and health connections
periods.activity_title: Local, Plant-Based, and Why It Matters
periods.activity_description: Students analyse the chapter's argument for eating locally grown and plant-based food by connecting it to three earlier chapter threads: regional food diversity, nutrient value, and food miles. Groups construct a reasoned written argument for or against the chapter's recommendation, using chapter evidence only.

roles.role_description: Each group writes a structured three-sentence argument — claim, evidence from the chapter, and implication for health or environment — either supporting or complicating the chapter's recommendation.
Facilitates the argument construction by asking groups to identify which chapter section provides their evidence, preventing unsupported claims.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the chapter's closing call to eat locally grown and plant-based food and asks: which parts of the chapter build this argument?
Groups draft their argument: claim (agree or add a nuance), evidence from a named chapter section, and implication for health or environment.
Groups share arguments; class notes which chapter sections were cited most and which arguments were best supported by evidence.
Teacher connects food wastage to food miles and nutrient value, noting the chapter's call to value farmers' labour as part of mindful eating.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit asks students to synthesise evidence from multiple chapter sections into a reasoned argument — a higher-order task that consolidates the analytical stage. Watch for groups who make strong claims without citing a specific chapter section; insist on evidence-grounded reasoning. The chapter does not forbid non-plant foods, so groups who write nuanced arguments (e.g., animal sources remain important for specific nutrients like Vitamin D) are demonstrating sophisticated engagement with the content and should be acknowledged.
homework: Read the nutritional label on any packaged food at home. Note two nutrients listed and look up which deficiency disease each prevents, using your nutrient chart.

periods.stage_label: Analyse food systems and health connections
periods.activity_title: Connecting Diet, Diversity, and Health: A Chapter Thread
periods.activity_description: Students construct a visual thread diagram linking the chapter's three main ideas — food diversity across regions, nutrient functions and testing, and balanced dietary choices — showing how each idea supports the others. The teacher guides the connection-making, ensuring that the final diagram represents the chapter's integrated argument.

roles.role_description: Leads the class through the thread diagram construction, modelling how to draw an arrow between concepts and narrate the connection aloud.
Each student builds their own thread diagram in their notebook, adding connection arrows and one-phrase labels for each link.

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws three nodes on the board — food diversity, nutrients, balanced diet — and asks: can you draw one arrow between any two of these and explain it?
Students build their own thread diagrams, adding sub-concepts (e.g., regional crops, deficiency diseases, food miles) as satellites around the three main nodes.
Two or three students describe one connection from their diagram; class evaluates whether the connection is supported by the chapter.
Teacher names the chapter's central argument: food diversity, nutrient knowledge, and dietary choices are connected, and understanding this connection is what mindful eating means.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit prepares students for the synthesis unit by having them articulate the chapter's internal logic in their own spatial representation. Students sometimes draw arrows prolifically without labelling them; require at least a two-word phrase on every arrow to ensure the connection is genuinely articulated, not decorative. This is also a good checkpoint before the synthesis unit: a student whose diagram links regional crops to nutrient availability to deficiency prevention is ready; a student whose diagram has only isolated nodes needs a brief conversation.

periods.stage_label: Analyse food systems and health connections

roles.role_description: Groups analyse the scenario, identify the nutritional problems, connect them to food system causes, and produce a written recommendation with evidence from the chapter's full content.
Introduces the scenario, clarifies that all chapter content is available as evidence, and facilitates a final class-wide sharing of recommendations.

periods.activity_description: Students receive a set of five 'patient profile cards' describing real-sounding but fictitious patients in a small district hospital canteen — a recovering child with anaemia in a jowar-growing district, a teenager athlete from a coastal fishing village, an elderly person in a Himalayan town with early signs of goitre, a young mother in a sugarcane-farming belt who relies heavily on processed snacks, and a construction worker in an urban area who skips meals. For each patient, groups must (a) identify which nutrients are most urgently needed and why, (b) choose three specific foods available in that patient's region that would address the deficiency or need, (c) run a quick paper analysis to confirm which of two unlabelled 'canteen food samples' (described on a data strip) contains starch, fat, or protein using the test logic from the chapter, and (d) flag any junk-food traps or high-food-miles risks on the proposed menu. A whole-class gallery of decisions is then interrogated: the teacher poses two cross-patient challenges that force students to articulate why the same nutrient can come from completely different regional foods, and why a balanced diet looks different in different contexts. The closing reflection names exactly what made the task solvable — the chapter's interlocking ideas — without rehearsing them as a list.
periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis unit tasks groups with advising a hospital canteen by diagnosing patient nutrient needs, interpreting food-test data, selecting regionally appropriate foods, and flagging junk-food or food-miles risks — drawing on the chapter's full interlocking ideas in one novel setting. The critical facilitation moves are the two cross-patient gallery challenges (see material: 'Cross-patient challenge prompts') and the closing patient-by-patient naming of what the class actually did, which should feel earned rather than list-like. Patient profile cards, food-sample data strips, and the decision sheet template are all prepared in advance (see materials).
materials: Five patient profile cards (see visual aid: 'Patient profile cards')
Two canteen food-sample data strips (see visual aid: 'Canteen food-sample data strips') — one strip per group, same two items for all groups
Blank decision sheet per group (see visual aid: 'Group decision sheet template')
Blackboard or large sheet of paper for the whole-class gallery — one row per patient group
Cross-patient challenge prompts (see visual aid: 'Cross-patient challenge prompts')

time_bands.activity: Teacher places a patient profile card and a food-sample data strip face-down on each group's desk. Without framing what the chapter covered, the teacher says: 'A small hospital canteen has asked us to advise on meals for five patients. Each group has one patient and two mystery food items the canteen already stocks. Your job is to work out what this patient needs, whether these items help, and what three regional foods you would add to the menu.' Cards are turned over. Teacher reads the two canteen food-sample test results aloud once so all groups hear the same data, then instructs groups to begin.

Groups work on their decision sheets. They first identify the nutrient gap from the symptom on the patient card, name the deficiency disease or health risk it signals, and select three specific foods available in the patient's region that address the gap — anchoring choices to the crops or food traditions of that location. They then interpret the food-sample data strip using the test logic: determine which of the two canteen items contains starch, fat, or protein, and decide whether each item belongs on this patient's tray or should be limited. Finally they flag any junk-food concern or high-food-miles risk in what they have proposed. Teacher circulates, asking probing questions: 'What symptom told you which nutrient was missing?' and 'Does that food actually grow in that region?' and 'Which test result are you reading to say fat is present?'

Each group writes their patient's name and three key decisions (nutrient identified, regional food chosen, canteen item verdict) on the blackboard gallery row. Once all five rows are up, teacher poses two cross-patient challenges to the whole class: first, 'Two patients both need a mineral — the child in the jowar district and the elder in the Himalayan town. Their minerals are different and their sources are very different. Why does the solution look so different for each?' Second, 'One group flagged a food-miles risk in their recommendation. Another group's recommended food travels even further but they did not flag it — should they have?' Class responds briefly; teacher steers without resolving for them, pressing for reasoning tied to the chapter's ideas.

Teacher closes by naming, patient by patient, what the class actually did: 'To advise the anaemic child, you connected a symptom to a nutrient, found a regional source, and used a test result to evaluate a canteen item — that is the chapter working as a whole. To advise the Himalayan elder, you had to know that some protective nutrients require fortified sources because local soil lacks them — that is why the chapter has both regional food diversity and the iodine-salt story. Every patient forced you to use a different part of the chapter, and none of them let you use just one part.' Teacher then states the chapter's central insight in one sentence: food choices are mindful when they draw together what grows locally, what the body specifically needs, and how far food travels to reach the plate — and this class has just demonstrated that.

visual_aids.title: Patient profile cards — format note
visual_aids.text: Each card is hand-written on an index card or half-sheet. It states the patient's name, age, location and dominant local crop, current typical daily diet, physical activity level, and one observable symptom or health need described in plain language. The card does NOT name the deficiency — students must infer it.

visual_aids.title: Patient profile cards
visual_aids.table:
Card | Patient & setting | Diet | Activity | Symptom
1 | Child, recovering patient, jowar-growing district | Predominantly jowar-based with very little green leafy vegetables or pulses | Low activity (bed rest) | Pale gums and fatigue, tires easily on minor exertion
2 | Teenager, athlete, coastal fishing village | Rice and fish-based but meals are often skipped before training | High physical activity | Frequent muscle cramps and slower recovery after exercise
3 | Elderly person, Himalayan town | Relies on locally grown cereals and dairy; rarely eats processed or iodised products | Low activity | Visible swelling at the front of the neck, sluggishness

visual_aids.table:
Nutrient needed and why | Regional food that provides it | Test evidence for nutrient presence | Junk-food or high-food-miles risk flagged
(identify from patient symptom) | (must be available in patient's region) | (cite which test result and what it shows) | (note any concern with proposed menu items)

visual_aids.title: Cross-patient challenge prompts
visual_aids.table:
Use these two prompts during the gallery interrogation phase. Do not resolve them for students — steer toward reasoning tied to the chapter's ideas
Challenge | Prompt (read aloud) | Target insight
1 | 'Two patients both need a mineral — the child in the jowar district and the elder in the Himalayan town. Their minerals are different and their sources are very different. Why does the solution look so different for each?' | 'Local and minimally processed' is not a universal rule; some protective nutrients require fortified or non-plant sources because local soil lacks them. A good comparison is iron from green leafy vegetables, regionally available, versus iodine from iodised salt, processed but necessary
2 | 'One group flagged a food-miles risk in their recommendation. Another group's recommended food travels even further but they did not flag it — should they have?' | Food-miles reasoning must be applied consistently and weighed against nutritional necessity; students must articulate the trade-off rather than apply a blanket rule

visual_aids.title: Gallery logistics and redirects
visual_aids.text: If groups are more than five, two groups may share a card and compare recommendations at the gallery stage. During group work, redirect students who chose regionally implausible foods by asking 'What grows there?' and redirect students uncertain about test results by asking 'Which test result tells you fat is present?'

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students record their own food habits, map traditional foods and crops across Indian states, and examine how cooking practices have changed over time due to technology and transport.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can describe how local crop availability, climate, cultural traditions, and historical change shape what people eat in different regions of India, giving specific examples from at least two states.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Classify nutrients by function and source
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students classify carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins, and minerals by function and source using the chapter's nutrient chart, historical deficiency cases, and a diagnosis-style survey activity.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can classify the major nutrients by their function and Indian food sources, match specific nutrient deficiencies to their symptoms, and recommend a dietary change to address a named deficiency.

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students perform the iodine test for starch and the paper-patch test for fat, observe the teacher demonstration of the protein test, and complete a three-test comparison table identifying which foods contain multiple nutrients.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can carry out the iodine and paper-patch tests, record and interpret colour or texture changes as evidence of a specific nutrient, and use a completed comparison table to identify foods that contain more than one testable nutrient.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Evaluate dietary quality and food choices
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students evaluate their own food record against balanced diet criteria, compare the nutritional profiles of junk food and whole foods using chapter data, and assess millets as nutri-cereals suited to varied climatic zones.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can evaluate a given diet against balanced diet criteria, use nutritional data to distinguish junk food from whole food, and justify why millets qualify as nutri-cereals by citing their nutrient content and cultivation adaptability.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Analyse food systems and health connections
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students map the wheat-to-chapati supply chain and evaluate food miles, construct evidence-based arguments for local and plant-based food choices, build a thread diagram connecting chapter concepts, and synthesise all chapter content through an integrative community health scenario.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can analyse the nutritional components and regional diversity of food together — tracing how supply chain length, food system choices, and dietary decisions interact to affect both personal health and community wellbeing — and produce a reasoned recommendation using evidence from across the chapter.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe how local crop availability, climate, cultural traditions, and historical change shape what people eat in different regions of India, giving specific examples from at least two states.

competency.competency_text: Examine food diversity through the dimensions of sources, nutrients, climatic conditions, and regional diets.

assessment_items.question_text: Punjab's traditional food includes makki di roti and sarson da saag, while Karnataka's traditional food includes ragi mudde and dosa. What is the main reason these two states have such different traditional foods?

options.label: A
options.text: Karnataka receives more rainfall than Punjab, so Karnataka's food contains more water.

options.label: B
options.text: People in different states have different taste preferences and nothing more.

options.label: C
options.text: Punjab and Karnataka have different religions, so their food rules differ.

options.label: D
options.text: The crops grown in each state depend on local soil and climate, and traditional food is built around those crops.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student recognises that food differs by region but reduces the explanation to taste preference alone, missing the structural crop-climate-food chain the chapter establishes.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student attempts a climate-based explanation but focuses on a single physical variable (rainfall and water content) rather than the crop-cultivation pathway that links climate to food.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student confuses cultural tradition with religious dietary rules, collapsing the chapter's distinction between cultural/taste preferences and the agricultural basis of traditional food.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who have personal experience of regional food differences (from travel or family background) can draw on that experience as a starting point before applying the chapter's crop-climate explanation. Students less familiar with these specific states can reason from the general principle: what grows locally is what gets cooked locally.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe how local crop availability, climate, cultural traditions, and historical change shape what people eat in different regions of India, giving specific examples from at least two states.

competency.competency_text: Examine food diversity through the dimensions of sources, nutrients, climatic conditions, and regional diets.

assessment_items.question_text: Cooking practices in India have shifted from the chulha and sil-batta to the gas stove and electric grinder. According to the chapter, which combination of factors best explains why this change happened?

options.label: A
options.text: People became lazy and stopped wanting to cook traditionally.

options.label: B
options.text: Technological development, improved transportation, and better communication made modern tools available and affordable.

options.label: C
options.text: Traditional cooking methods produced food that tasted worse than modern methods.

options.label: D
options.text: Traditional tools broke down and were never repaired.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student attributes the change to individual behaviour (laziness) rather than structural factors like technology and infrastructure, showing a personal rather than systemic frame of reasoning.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student accepts that change occurred but misidentifies the mechanism as equipment failure rather than the availability of alternatives driven by technological and economic development.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student focuses on sensory quality as the driver of change, bypassing the chapter's explanation of technology, transport, and communication as the structural causes.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who have seen both traditional and modern cooking tools in their own homes or extended families can ground their answer in lived observation before applying the chapter's explanation. Students who have only seen modern tools can reason about what would have had to change for new tools to become available everywhere.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify nutrients by function and source
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify the major nutrients by their function and Indian food sources, match specific nutrient deficiencies to their symptoms, and recommend a dietary change to address a named deficiency.

competency.competency_text: Identify and classify the major nutrients, describe their functions and sources with reference to Indian foods, and connect nutrient deficiency to specific diseases.

assessment_items.question_text: A child living in a mountain village is found to have swelling at the front of the neck. According to the chapter, which nutrient is most likely deficient in the local diet, and which food addition would directly address this?

options.label: A
options.text: Calcium is deficient; the child should drink more milk.

options.label: B
options.text: Iodine is deficient; the family should use iodised salt instead of untreated salt.

options.label: C
options.text: Iron is deficient; the child should eat more green leafy vegetables.

options.label: D
options.text: Vitamin C is deficient; the child should eat amla and guava.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student correctly identifies a mineral deficiency but confuses iodine with iron, likely because both are minerals and both appear in the chapter's deficiency chart; this is a within-chapter concept confusion.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student recognises that a deficiency is present but misidentifies it as Vitamin C (perhaps recalling the earlier scurvy case), conflating a vitamin deficiency with a mineral deficiency.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student correctly identifies a mineral but selects calcium, possibly associating neck symptoms with bone problems (rickets/calcium) rather than reading the goitre symptom description carefully.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who recall the chapter's historical case about Indian scientists and goitre will have a strong contextual anchor. Students who approach this analytically can eliminate options by matching the symptom (neck swelling) to the deficiency disease (goitre) and then to the nutrient (iodine) using the chart.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify nutrients by function and source
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify the major nutrients by their function and Indian food sources, match specific nutrient deficiencies to their symptoms, and recommend a dietary change to address a named deficiency.

competency.competency_text: Identify and classify the major nutrients, describe their functions and sources with reference to Indian foods, and connect nutrient deficiency to specific diseases.

assessment_items.question_text: Carbohydrates and fats are both called energy-giving foods in the chapter. Which statement correctly distinguishes their roles as described in the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: Both carbohydrates and fats perform identical functions, so there is no practical difference between them.

options.label: B
options.text: Carbohydrates build and repair body tissues; fats provide energy for daily activity.

options.label: C
options.text: Carbohydrates protect the body from diseases; fats help in growth.

options.label: D
options.text: Carbohydrates provide energy including instant energy from glucose; fats provide energy and act as stored energy, giving warmth especially in cold conditions.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has swapped the functions of macronutrients, assigning the body-building function of proteins to carbohydrates, suggesting the three-category classification has not been consolidated.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student assigns the protective function of vitamins and minerals to carbohydrates and the body-building function of proteins to fats, indicating a general confusion across all nutrient function categories.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may have correctly identified both as energy-giving foods but over-generalised this shared label to mean they are indistinguishable, missing the chapter's distinction about stored energy, warmth, and instant glucose energy.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can connect the laddoo-in-winter example (fats for warmth and stored energy) and the tired-when-skipping-meals example (carbohydrates for instant energy) as concrete anchors before choosing between the options.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify nutrients by function and source
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify the major nutrients by their function and Indian food sources, match specific nutrient deficiencies to their symptoms, and recommend a dietary change to address a named deficiency.

competency.competency_text: Identify and classify the major nutrients, describe their functions and sources with reference to Indian foods, and connect nutrient deficiency to specific diseases.

assessment_items.question_text: A young child is diagnosed with rickets. Using the chapter's nutrient information, identify the deficient nutrient, name one unusual source of this nutrient that does not come from food, and suggest one dietary source the family could add.
expected_elements: Identification of Vitamin D as the nutrient deficient in rickets.
Naming sunlight as a non-food source through which the body synthesises Vitamin D.
Suggesting at least one chapter-listed dietary source such as milk, butter, fish, or eggs.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who recall the Vitamin D entry in the chapter's nutrient chart will work systematically; students who remember the chapter's comment that 'not all nutrients come from plants and animals' will find the sunlight point naturally. Both pathways arrive at a complete answer.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can carry out the iodine and paper-patch tests, record and interpret colour or texture changes as evidence of a specific nutrient, and use a completed comparison table to identify foods that contain more than one testable nutrient.

competency.competency_text: Identify and classify the major nutrients, describe their functions and sources with reference to Indian foods, and conduct empirical tests for starch, fat, and protein.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Food sample | Iodine test result | Paper-patch test result | Protein test result
Boiled rice | Blue-black colour | No oily patch | No violet colour
Peanut | No blue-black colour | Oily translucent patch | Violet colour
Cucumber | No blue-black colour | No oily patch | No violet colour
Potato | Blue-black colour | No oily patch | No violet colour
assessment_items.question_text: Refer to the table provided. A student completes the three nutrient tests for four food samples. Which food sample contains more than one testable nutrient, and what are those nutrients?

options.label: A
options.text: Boiled rice — it contains starch and protein.

options.label: B
options.text: Cucumber — it contains fat and protein.

options.label: C
options.text: Peanut — it contains fat and protein.

options.label: D
options.text: Potato — it contains starch and fat.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student correctly reads the iodine test for boiled rice but then incorrectly assigns a protein result, likely confusing boiled rice with boiled gram or misreading the protein column in the table.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student correctly identifies potato's starch result but then adds fat, possibly because potato is starchy and dense and the student assumes density implies fat, showing a reasoning error not grounded in the test evidence.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student selects cucumber, which shows no positive result for any test in the table, suggesting the student may be guessing or confusing the absence of a result with a positive one.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who worked through the comparison table during the nutrient testing units will recognise the pattern immediately from their own recorded data. Students approaching the table fresh can read across rows and count positive results to identify which food has more than one.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can carry out the iodine and paper-patch tests, record and interpret colour or texture changes as evidence of a specific nutrient, and use a completed comparison table to identify foods that contain more than one testable nutrient.

competency.competency_text: Identify and classify the major nutrients, describe their functions and sources with reference to Indian foods, and conduct empirical tests for starch, fat, and protein.

assessment_items.question_text: A student presses a piece of butter onto plain paper and holds it up to light. The patch does not disappear when left to dry. What does this result confirm, and which test is the student performing?

options.label: A
options.text: The butter contains fat; this is the paper-patch test.

options.label: B
options.text: The butter contains protein; this is the protein test.

options.label: C
options.text: The butter contains starch; this is the iodine test.

options.label: D
options.text: The butter contains water; this is the paper-patch test.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student confuses the observable indicator (patch persists on paper) with the starch test indicator (blue-black colour from iodine), conflating two entirely different tests.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student correctly names the paper-based method but misidentifies the nutrient detected, possibly confusing fat detection with protein detection because both are associated with animal foods like butter and cheese.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student identifies the correct test name but misattributes the persistent patch to water rather than fat, possibly because the chapter warns that a water stain fades — the student may have remembered 'water' from that explanation but applied it incorrectly.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who recall the chapter's explicit distinction between a water stain (fades on drying) and an oily patch (persists) will confidently eliminate the water option. Students who approach this procedurally can reason: what leaves a permanent oily mark on paper — fat.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can carry out the iodine and paper-patch tests, record and interpret colour or texture changes as evidence of a specific nutrient, and use a completed comparison table to identify foods that contain more than one testable nutrient.

competency.competency_text: Identify and classify the major nutrients, describe their functions and sources with reference to Indian foods, and conduct empirical tests for starch, fat, and protein.

assessment_items.question_text: Two students test the same food sample. Student A performs the iodine test and observes no colour change. Student B performs the paper-patch test and observes a translucent patch that stays after drying. What can each student conclude about the food sample, and what does combining their results tell us that neither test alone could?
expected_elements: Student A's result (no colour change with iodine) means starch is absent in the sample.
Student B's result (persistent translucent patch) means fat is present in the sample.

Combining the results tells us the food contains fat but not starch — something that neither single test can determine on its own, because each test only reveals the presence or absence of one specific nutrient.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who approach this by working through each test result separately before combining them will find the structure of the question helpful. Students who think about the comparison table they completed — where each column showed one nutrient independently — can apply the same logic here.

assessment_items.stage_label: Evaluate dietary quality and food choices
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can evaluate a given diet against balanced diet criteria, use nutritional data to distinguish junk food from whole food, and justify why millets qualify as nutri-cereals by citing their nutrient content and cultivation adaptability.

competency.competency_text: Identify and classify the major nutrients, describe their functions and sources, and distinguish a balanced diet from junk food.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Food (per 100 g) | Calories (kcal) | Fat (g) | Protein (g) | Dietary fibre (g)
Potato wafers | 536 | 35 | Low | Low
Roasted chana | 355 | 6.26 | 18.64 | 16.8
assessment_items.question_text: Refer to the table provided. A student argues that potato wafers are a better energy food than roasted chana because they have more calories. Using the table, explain why this reasoning is incomplete when evaluating which food better supports a balanced diet.

options.label: A
options.text: Calories are not relevant to a balanced diet, so the student's entire argument is irrelevant.

options.label: B
options.text: The student ignores that roasted chana provides significantly more protein and dietary fibre, which support growth and digestive health alongside energy.

options.label: C
options.text: The student is correct — higher calories always mean a better food choice for energy.

options.label: D
options.text: The student is wrong because potato wafers contain no energy at all.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student accepts the calorie-only logic without questioning it, showing they have not yet incorporated the multi-nutrient view of dietary quality that the chapter builds through the balanced diet definition.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student correctly rejects the wafers but over-corrects by stating they contain no energy, confusing 'not the best choice' with 'contains nothing' — a factual error about the calorie data in the table.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student dismisses the calorie argument entirely rather than integrating it appropriately, showing an inability to hold multiple nutritional criteria simultaneously.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who worked through the numerical comparison of the two foods will have the table data in memory and can locate the protein and fibre columns directly. Students who approach this conceptually can reason: a balanced diet needs multiple nutrients, so a food that only provides calories is incomplete by definition.

assessment_items.stage_label: Evaluate dietary quality and food choices
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can evaluate a given diet against balanced diet criteria, use nutritional data to distinguish junk food from whole food, and justify why millets qualify as nutri-cereals by citing their nutrient content and cultivation adaptability.

competency.competency_text: Identify and classify the major nutrients, describe their functions and sources, and distinguish a balanced diet from junk food.

assessment_items.question_text: Ragi, jowar, bajra, and sanwa are described as nutri-cereals. Which combination of properties best justifies this name according to the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: They are cereals that are only grown in one specific climate zone, making them rare and nutritious.

options.label: B
options.text: They are cereals that are rich in vitamins, minerals including iron and calcium, and dietary fibre, and can be grown across a range of climatic conditions.

options.label: C
options.text: They are cereals that have more calories than wheat and rice, giving more energy per meal.

options.label: D
options.text: They are cereals that were recently introduced to India and have high protein content.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student associates 'nutri' with scarcity rather than nutrient richness, and inverts the chapter's claim about climatic adaptability — millets are described as growing across varied conditions, not a single zone.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student focuses solely on caloric value as the marker of nutritional quality, applying the same incomplete reasoning the chapter's junk food comparison was designed to challenge.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student correctly associates millets with nutrition but introduces two factual errors from outside the chapter: that millets were recently introduced (the chapter explicitly states they have been part of India's diet for centuries) and that the key nutrient is protein rather than iron, calcium, and fibre.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who connected the millet evaluation table from the assessment stage to this question will recall the specific nutrients cited. Students who approach the term 'nutri-cereal' analytically can decompose it: 'nutri' signals nutrient richness, and the chapter specifies which nutrients and why the crop is considered adaptable.

assessment_items.stage_label: Evaluate dietary quality and food choices
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can evaluate a given diet against balanced diet criteria, use nutritional data to distinguish junk food from whole food, and justify why millets qualify as nutri-cereals by citing their nutrient content and cultivation adaptability.

competency.competency_text: Identify and classify the major nutrients, describe their functions and sources, and distinguish a balanced diet from junk food.

assessment_items.question_text: A student's weekly food diary shows the following: chapati, rice, and potato every day; milk occasionally; almost no pulses, eggs, fruits, or vegetables. Using the chapter's definition of a balanced diet, identify two nutrient gaps in this diet and name one specific food the student could add to address each gap.
expected_elements: Identification of protein deficiency — the diet has almost no pulses, eggs, milk, or other protein sources — with a suggested addition such as dal, paneer, eggs, or rajma.

Identification of at least one vitamin or mineral deficiency — the diet lacks fruits and vegetables — with a suggested addition citing a specific Indian food from the chapter's nutrient chart (e.g., amla for Vitamin C, green leafy vegetables for iron, carrot for Vitamin A).
Both suggested foods should be drawn from the chapter's named sources, not invented examples.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who annotated their own food records during the evaluation stage will apply the same process here to a new record. Students who find it easier to work from the nutrient chart can scan it column by column for nutrients that the described diet cannot supply.

assessment_items.stage_label: Analyse food systems and health connections
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can analyse the nutritional components and regional diversity of food together — tracing how supply chain length, food system choices, and dietary decisions interact to affect both personal health and community wellbeing — and produce a reasoned recommendation using evidence from across the chapter.

competency.competency_text: Identify and classify the major nutrients, describe their functions and sources, and explain how food diversity and balanced dietary choices affect health.

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter states that reducing food miles benefits health, environment, and local farmers. Which of the following best explains the health benefit of reducing food miles, as argued in the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: Food produced locally always contains more protein than food transported from another state.

options.label: B
options.text: Food that travels fewer kilometres is cheaper, so families can buy more of it.

options.label: C
options.text: Food that travels fewer steps in the supply chain reaches the consumer fresher, retaining more of its nutrients.

options.label: D
options.text: Reducing food miles eliminates the need for food testing because local food is safer.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student identifies an economic benefit of reduced food miles but substitutes it for the health benefit, showing they recall the multi-benefit argument but cannot distinguish which benefit is which.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student correctly associates local food with better nutrition but over-claims: the chapter argues that freshness preserves nutrients, not that local food is categorically higher in a specific macronutrient like protein.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student conflates two unrelated concepts — food miles and food safety testing — showing a generalisation error that collapses the chapter's supply chain argument into the unrelated topic of nutrient testing.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who traced the supply chain flow diagram will recall the nutrient-freshness link as an explicit annotation they were asked to make. Students reasoning from the chapter's vitamin discussion can connect the vitamin-loss-during-cooking note to the broader principle that nutrients degrade over time and distance.

assessment_items.stage_label: Analyse food systems and health connections
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can analyse the nutritional components and regional diversity of food together — tracing how supply chain length, food system choices, and dietary decisions interact to affect both personal health and community wellbeing — and produce a reasoned recommendation using evidence from across the chapter.

competency.competency_text: Examine food diversity through the dimensions of sources, nutrients, climatic conditions, and regional diets.

assessment_items.question_text: A school canteen currently serves only packaged biscuits and carbonated drinks. Using reasoning that combines the chapter's nutrient knowledge, food diversity argument, and food miles concept, which change would most comprehensively improve the canteen's offering?

options.label: A
options.text: Add roasted chana, fresh seasonal fruit, and a millet-based option sourced from nearby farms.

options.label: B
options.text: Add Vitamin C supplements so that students compensate for what the biscuits lack.

options.label: C
options.text: Replace biscuits with potato wafers because wafers have more calories.

options.label: D
options.text: Replace carbonated drinks with fruit juice imported from another country.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student attempts to improve nutrition by adding fruit juice but selects an imported source, missing the food miles argument entirely and showing that nutrient thinking and supply chain thinking have not been integrated.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student identifies the nutrient gap but addresses it through a supplement rather than a whole food, bypassing both the food diversity argument and the food miles concept — showing nutrient knowledge applied in isolation.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student substitutes one high-fat, low-nutrient food for another, possibly recalling that wafers were described as high in calories without retaining the chapter's evaluation of what a balanced diet actually requires.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who built the thread diagram connecting food diversity, nutrients, and food systems will approach this option-by-option by asking: does this address nutrients? Does it reflect food diversity? Does it consider the supply chain? Students who focus on a single criterion will arrive at a partially correct but not comprehensively supported answer.

assessment_items.stage_label: Analyse food systems and health connections
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can analyse the nutritional components and regional diversity of food together — tracing how supply chain length, food system choices, and dietary decisions interact to affect both personal health and community wellbeing — and produce a reasoned recommendation using evidence from across the chapter.

competency.competency_text: Identify and classify the major nutrients, describe their functions and sources, and explain how food diversity and balanced dietary choices affect health.

assessment_items.question_text: A state government wants to improve the health of school-aged children. It is considering two options: Option 1 — distribute Vitamin C tablets to all children daily; Option 2 — support local farmers to supply seasonal fruits and vegetables to school mid-day meals. Using the chapter's arguments about nutrients, food sources, and food miles, evaluate which option better serves children's health and explain your reasoning.
look_for: A clear evaluative stance: the student recommends Option 2 (or provides a nuanced argument) and supports it with specific reasoning rather than stating a preference without evidence.
Reference to the chapter's nutrient argument: Option 2 provides multiple nutrients simultaneously (carbohydrates, vitamins, minerals, fibre) rather than a single vitamin supplement.
Reference to the food miles / supply chain argument: locally sourced food retains more nutrients and supports local farmers — both points made in the chapter.
Acknowledgement that Option 1 addresses only one deficiency while a varied diet of fresh food prevents multiple deficiency diseases at once.
Use of specific foods or nutrients from the chapter (not invented) as evidence.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who express their argument as a simple preference ('Option 2 is better because vegetables are natural') should be prompted by the teacher to identify which chapter argument supports that claim. Students who work from the nutrient chart first, then add the food miles argument, will produce a richer response — both are valid entry points.

assessment_items.stage_label: Analyse food systems and health connections
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can analyse the nutritional components and regional diversity of food together — tracing how supply chain length, food system choices, and dietary decisions interact to affect both personal health and community wellbeing — and produce a reasoned recommendation using evidence from across the chapter.

competency.competency_text: Identify and classify the major nutrients, describe their functions and sources with reference to Indian foods, conduct simple nutrient tests, and explain how food diversity and balanced dietary choices affect health.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Community | Staple food in use | Observed health symptom | Traditional crop historically grown | Supply chain: local or long-distance
Hill village, Himalayan region | Only polished white rice and packaged noodles | Several children with swollen necks and poor night vision | Millets, green leafy vegetables, apricots | Mostly long-distance packaged food
Coastal town, southern India | Rice, some fish, packaged snacks | Children tire easily, pale appearance | Coconut, drumstick leaves, sesame | Mixed — some local, much packaged
Dryland farming area, central India | Sorghum (jowar), bajra, seasonal vegetables | Generally good health reported | Jowar, bajra, seasonal pulses | Mostly local
assessment_items.task: Three communities in different parts of India are described in the table. For each community, use the chapter's content to complete the following: (1) identify the nutrient or nutrients most likely deficient based on the observed symptoms, (2) explain how the shift away from traditional crops and toward long-distance packaged food may have caused this deficiency, (3) recommend two specific foods from the chapter that could address the deficiency and are consistent with that community's traditional food base or climate, and (4) for the third community, explain what their food choices are doing right and why maintaining a short supply chain matters for their continued health.
assessment_items.scaffold: Work through each community row by row. For the first two communities: name the deficiency disease and the missing nutrient before suggesting foods. For the third community: identify which nutrients their staple crops provide and connect that to the absence of reported health problems. In your recommendation, name the food, the nutrient it provides, and one reason it fits the community's climate or food tradition.
format_of_output: Written response structured community by community
Each community addressed in a separate paragraph
Specific food names and nutrient names required — general statements such as 'eat healthy food' are not sufficient

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Data interpretation task (provided table or graph)
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The final stage's implied LO requires students to reason simultaneously across nutrient science, food diversity, and food system factors — a data table with three contrasting communities forces all three analytical threads to be applied together, making it the most direct demonstration vehicle for the integrated operation the dissolution test names.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response demonstrates that the student can read symptom data to identify nutrient deficiencies, connect food system choices (supply chain length, crop abandonment) to those deficiencies, recommend contextually appropriate foods using chapter evidence, and evaluate a community's food practice positively when the evidence supports it — all simultaneously.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold directs students through a row-by-row structure to prevent them from treating the three communities as a single undifferentiated problem. The final instruction — to explain what the third community is doing right — tests whether students can apply the chapter's argument in a positive evaluative direction, not only as a diagnosis of failure. A student who addresses only the first two communities has not completed the task.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses name specific nutrients and specific Indian food sources from the chapter for each community, make an explicit connection between supply chain length and nutrient loss or retention, and explain the third community's health positively by citing their millet/pulse/local food combination. Weak responses use general language ('eat more vegetables', 'avoid junk food') without naming nutrients or foods, or diagnose the first two communities correctly but fail to address the third community's positive case.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who prefer to work through the nutrient chart column by column before engaging with the scenario will find the symptom-to-nutrient mapping accessible. Students who think in terms of food systems first (from the food miles and supply chain units) can use that lens to enter the task and then ground their recommendations in the nutrient chart. Both pathways produce a complete response.
